context: You work for a company that has offices in several countries. Your manager has written to offer you a two-year post abroad.

paragraphs: Following your work on the Samarkand project, we would like to offer you a two-year post in our Warsaw office, beginning in September. The company would cover your flights, your accommodation for the first three months and a language course.
It is a significant decision, so please take time to consider it. Let me know your thoughts and any questions you have.

task11: Write a message to your friend. Tell them about the offer, write about your feelings and say whether you are going to accept it.
task12: Write an email to your manager. Write about your feelings, say whether you accept the offer, and ask any questions you still have.
part2_question: Is it better to build your career in your own country or abroad?

task11: Sit down for this one: they have offered me two years in Warsaw, starting in September. I am excited and terrified in equal measure. The package looks generous and I would be mad to refuse it, so I think I am going to say yes. Coffee tomorrow?
task12: Thank you for the offer of the Warsaw post, and for the confidence in my work that it represents. I was delighted to receive it and, having discussed it with my family, I am pleased to accept.

September would suit me well, as it gives me time to hand over the Samarkand project properly rather than leaving it half finished. I would also like to begin the language course before I leave, if a place can be arranged.

I do have three questions. Would the company help with a visa for my wife, who hopes to work in Poland? Is there a budget for travel home at the end of the first year? And will my current role be held open for my return in two years' time?
part2: For ambitious people in a smaller economy, the question of whether to build a career at home or abroad arrives sooner or later. Both routes work, and the choice is less permanent than it looks.

Going abroad offers scale. Larger markets mean larger projects, better equipment and colleagues at the top of the field, and a few years in that environment can accelerate a career by a decade. The money is usually better, and working in a second language is itself a lasting qualification.

Staying has quieter advantages that people undervalue. You already understand the market and the culture, your network is here, and in a growing economy a capable person reaches a senior position far younger than they would abroad. There is also the matter of being present for parents as they age, which no salary compensates for. A foreign posting teaches you how differently the same job can be done, which is hard to learn any other way.

My own view is that the strongest career is often both: experience abroad, then bring it home while the skills are still fresh. Returning with that experience is often what opens the most senior doors at home.
